items.text: Monitors your location, calls, or messages without your knowledge or consent
Controls or limits your access to money, credit cards, or financial accounts
Enforces rules about your appearance, movements, relationships, or speech
Isolates you from friends, family, or support systems
Uses children, pets, or shared assets as leverage or threats
Threatens negative consequences if you do not comply with their demands

result.description: A pattern of behavior designed to dominate, isolate, and control — often without physical violence. Recognized as a form of domestic abuse in several jurisdictions and increasingly named in law.

items.text: Denies events you know happened, or insists your memory or perception is wrong (gaslighting)
Blames you for their abusive behavior, or portrays themselves as the victim (DARVO)
Alternates between intense affection and sudden withdrawal or punishment
Recruits friends, family, or colleagues to pressure, surveil, or discredit you (flying monkeys)
Consistently reframes your reality, making you question your own judgment
Pursues re-engagement after periods of abandonment using promises, threats, or manufactured crises (hoovering)

result.description: Systematic distortion of reality and emotional manipulation that erodes self-trust over time. These patterns can be as damaging as physical abuse and are often more difficult to name and document.

items.text: Has demanded or taken access to your device, accounts, email, or passwords
You suspect monitoring software (stalkerware) has been installed on your device
Uses shared family plans, location sharing, or cloud accounts to track your location or activity
Contacts or harasses you across multiple platforms after you have blocked them on one
Has posted, threatened to post, or controls private images or recordings of you
Deletes messages or alters accounts to interfere with your ability to document what happened

result.description: Modern abusers use technology as a control vector — surveillance, harassment, and evidence interference can all occur digitally. These tactics often run in parallel with other forms of abuse and leave their own documentation trail.

workplace.statute: Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
workplace.extended_deadline_note: 300 days in states with a Fair Employment Practices Agency (FEPA)
workplace.scope: Prohibits employment discrimination based on sex. Workplace harassment and hostile work environment created by coercive tactics may give rise to a Title VII claim.
PTSD and other trauma-related conditions may constitute a covered disability. Employers must provide reasonable accommodation and may not retaliate for accommodation requests.
Entitles eligible employees to 12 weeks of unpaid leave for a serious health condition. Applies to employers with 50+ employees. Retaliation for exercising FMLA rights is prohibited.
Protects concerted activity and collective action by employees. Applies even without a union. Employer retaliation for organizing or collective complaint is an unfair labor practice.

whistleblower.scope: Protects employees of publicly traded companies who report mail, wire, bank, or securities fraud. Covers reports to federal agencies, Congress, or supervisors. Remedies include reinstatement, back pay, and attorney fees.

Provides financial awards (10–30% of sanctions over $1M) and anti-retaliation protections for reporting securities violations to the SEC. No filing deadline for the retaliation claim under some circuits.

Qui tam provision allows individuals to file suit on behalf of the government for fraud against federal programs. Whistleblowers can receive 15–30% of recovered funds. Anti-retaliation provision at § 3730(h).
Prohibits employer retaliation against workers who report workplace safety violations to OSHA. Strict 30-day filing window from the retaliatory act.
